name: Temperature
examples: Measure your temperature.
Let's check for a fever with a thermometer.
Please take a temperature reading.

name: Pulse / heart rate
examples: Check your pulse.
Measure your heart rate.
Let's count your heartbeat.

name: Blood pressure
examples: Measure your blood pressure.
Let's check your BP.
Take a reading with the blood-pressure cuff.

name: Respiratory rate
examples: Count your breaths per minute.
Measure your respiratory rate.
Let's check how fast you are breathing.

name: Oxygen saturation
examples: Check your oxygen saturation.
Measure your SpO2.
Use a finger pulse oximeter.
note: An oxygen-level measurement is not a request to give oxygen treatment.

name: Lung auscultation
examples: Let me listen to your lungs.
Check your breath sounds with a stethoscope.
Auscultate the chest.
note: Do not treat 'examine the chest' as automatically ordering imaging.

name: Ear examination
examples: Let me examine your ears.
Look inside the ear with an otoscope.
Check your eardrums.

name: Capillary refill
examples: Check capillary refill.
Press the nail bed and time how quickly the color returns.
Measure the capillary refill time.

name: Visual acuity
examples: Test your vision using an eye chart.
Measure your visual acuity.
Let's check how clearly you can read the chart.
note: Different from inspecting the eye or examining the retina.

name: Fundoscopic examination
examples: Examine the back of your eyes.
Perform fundoscopy.
Look at the retina and optic discs with an ophthalmoscope.

name: Eye examination
examples: Examine your eyes for redness.
Check your pupils with a penlight.
Inspect your eyes for irritation.
note: A broad eye request should not silently order visual acuity and fundoscopy too.

name: Neurovascular examination
examples: Check circulation and sensation in the injured foot.
Perform a neurovascular examination of the ankle.
Check the foot pulses and sensation.
note: Confirm the limb if it is not established in conversation.

name: Range of motion
examples: Assess the ankle's range of motion.
Check how far the injured joint can move.
Measure ankle movement with a goniometer.
note: Confirm the joint; account for case-specific pain and safety constraints.

name: Weight-bearing assessment
examples: Assess whether you can bear weight on the injured foot.
Check your ability to stand on that ankle.
Assess weight-bearing after the injury.
note: A history question about earlier walking is not itself a completed physical assessment.

name: Gait assessment
examples: Assess your gait.
Let me observe how you walk.
Examine your walking pattern.

name: Strength and reflex testing
examples: Test your leg strength and reflexes.
Perform a motor and reflex examination.
Check muscle power and tendon reflexes.
note: Do not assume an entire neurological examination was completed from one reflex test.

name: Functional assessment
examples: Assess how back pain affects your daily activities.
Review your ability to stand, dress and move around.
Perform a functional mobility assessment.

name: Joint examination
examples: Examine the swollen knee.
Check the painful joint for warmth and swelling.
Perform a joint examination.
note: Confirm the joint if unclear; this is not automatically joint-fluid sampling.

name: Breast examination
examples: With your consent, examine the breast lump.
Perform a clinical breast examination after consent.
Offer a chaperone and ask permission to examine the breast.
note: Offering or requesting consent must not automatically complete the examination.

name: Rash distribution assessment
examples: Check where the rash appears on your body.
Map the distribution of the rash.
Assess which skin areas are affected.

name: Skin scraping
examples: Take a skin scraping from the rash.
Collect a scraping to check for fungus.
Order a KOH preparation from the affected skin.
note: Specify the site; a particular preparation may require a subtype.

name: Chest X-ray
examples: Order a chest X-ray.
Get a CXR.
Request a chest radiograph.
note: An unspecified 'scan' needs clarification rather than selecting CT or X-ray.

name: Chest CT
examples: Order a CT of the chest.
Request a thoracic CT scan.
Get a chest CT to evaluate the lung lesion.
note: Do not silently add contrast or a pulmonary angiography protocol.

name: Spine MRI
examples: Order an MRI of the lumbar spine.
Request a spine MRI.
Get an MRI of the lower back.
note: Confirm the spinal region if not established.

name: Ultrasound
examples: Order an ultrasound of the breast lump.
Request ultrasound of the swollen joint.
Get an ultrasound of the affected area.
note: Body site is required; one generic ultrasound tool must not guess the organ.

name: Mammography
examples: Order diagnostic mammography.
Request a mammogram for this breast lump.
Get diagnostic breast X-ray imaging.

name: Biopsy
examples: Arrange a biopsy of the lung lesion.
Obtain a tissue sample from the breast lump.
Request a biopsy of the suspicious lesion.
note: Confirm site, procedure and consent. Link sampling and histopathology so one clinical order does not earn duplicate rewards.

name: Histopathology
examples: Send the biopsy for histopathology.
Examine the tissue sample under the microscope.
Request histological examination of the specimen.
note: Requires a tissue sample. Reviewing an existing report should not order another test.

name: Immunohistochemistry
examples: Order immunohistochemistry on the biopsy.
Request tumor immunostains.
Perform IHC to help classify the tissue.
note: Confirm the marker panel and specimen; distinguish broad IHC from a specific receptor panel.

name: ER / PR / HER2 testing
examples: Test the breast tumor for ER, PR and HER2.
Order breast cancer receptor testing.
Check estrogen, progesterone and HER2 receptor status.
note: A request for one marker should not automatically order or score all three.

name: Bone-marrow examination
examples: Arrange a bone-marrow examination.
Request a marrow aspirate for the abnormal blood counts.
Discuss and arrange a bone-marrow biopsy.
note: Aspirate and biopsy are related but distinct; confirm the requested procedure and consent.

name: Flow cytometry
examples: Order flow cytometry on the blood sample.
Request immunophenotyping of the abnormal cells.
Analyze the marrow cell populations with flow cytometry.
note: Confirm the specimen and requested analysis.

name: Complete blood count
examples: Order a complete blood count.
Check a CBC.
Get a full blood count.
note: 'Blood tests' alone should prompt clarification, not order an entire laboratory panel.

name: Blood smear
examples: Review a peripheral blood smear.
Order a blood film.
Examine the blood cells under a microscope.
note: Interpret 'review' as opening an existing result when one is already available.

name: Joint-fluid analysis
examples: Arrange aspiration and analysis of the swollen knee fluid.
Analyze the synovial fluid.
Send the joint aspirate for cell count and crystals.
note: Requires a specified joint and specimen; culture is a separate requested component.

name: Electrolytes
examples: Check serum electrolytes.
Measure sodium, potassium and chloride.
Order an electrolyte panel.
note: Do not silently expand this into every chemistry test.

name: Tumor mutation panel
examples: Sequence the tumor for somatic mutations.
Order a tumor mutation panel.
Request genomic profiling of the cancer tissue.
note: Different from inherited genetic testing or viral sequencing; confirm tumor specimen and panel.

name: Karyotype
examples: Order a karyotype.
Examine the chromosome number and large structural changes.
Request conventional chromosome analysis.
note: 'Chromosomal abnormalities' can mean karyotype, FISH or microarray; clarify when unspecified.

name: FISH
examples: Order FISH for the suspected rearrangement.
Use fluorescence in situ hybridization on the sample.
Request targeted FISH probes for the specified gene fusion.
note: The target/probe must be specified or established in context.

name: Molecular testing
examples: Test the blood sample for BCR-ABL1 by PCR.
Order a targeted molecular assay for the suspected gene fusion.
Request molecular testing for the specified hematologic mutation.
note: Very broad name: clarify target and method. Do not route every mention of PCR here.

name: Germline genetic testing
examples: After counseling and consent, order inherited cancer predisposition testing.
Test for a hereditary cancer syndrome.
Request a germline cancer gene panel.
note: Distinguish inherited variants from tumor-only mutations; establish consent and panel.

name: Family pedigree
examples: Build a three-generation family pedigree.
Map affected relatives in a family tree.
Take a structured family history for inherited conditions.

name: Genetic counseling
examples: Arrange genetic counseling before testing.
Discuss the implications and limitations of genetic testing.
Review inherited risks and testing choices with the patient.
note: Arranging a referral and completing a counseling discussion are not the same action.

name: Chromosomal microarray
examples: Order a chromosomal microarray.
Check for chromosome copy-number gains and losses using CMA.
Request microarray testing for deletions and duplications.
note: Not interchangeable with karyotype, sequencing or targeted FISH.

name: Gene sequencing
examples: Sequence the specified gene for the suspected inherited condition.
Order the relevant inherited-disorder gene panel.
Request gene sequencing for this familial condition.
note: 'Sequence it' or 'genetic test' is ambiguous. Confirm specimen, target and purpose.

name: Autoimmune antibodies
examples: Order rheumatoid factor and anti-CCP for the suspected arthritis.
Request the relevant autoimmune antibody tests.
Check the specified autoantibodies for this differential diagnosis.
note: Clarify which antibodies; do not interpret a vague request as every autoimmune test.

name: Inflammatory markers
examples: Check CRP and ESR.
Order inflammatory markers.
Measure C-reactive protein.
note: A request for CRP alone must not silently order ESR too.

name: Targeted allergy testing
examples: Test for specific IgE to the suspected pollen allergen.
Order targeted allergy testing for the suspected trigger.
Check sensitization to the specified allergen.
note: Confirm allergen and method; skin patch tests assess a different kind of allergy.

name: Gonorrhea NAAT
examples: Order a gonorrhea NAAT.
Test the appropriate sample for gonorrhea by PCR.
Request nucleic acid testing for Neisseria gonorrhoeae.
note: Establish sample site and consent. A combined STI panel is not automatic.

name: HIV testing
examples: With your consent, order an HIV test.
Request HIV antigen-antibody screening.
Discuss consent for HIV testing and then order the agreed test.
note: Confirm consent and test type; counseling alone is not a completed test.

name: Syphilis testing
examples: Order syphilis serology.
Test the blood sample for syphilis.
Request syphilis screening with consent.
note: Use the case's defined testing algorithm rather than inventing a test combination.

name: Stool pathogen testing
examples: Order a stool pathogen panel.
Test the stool for enteric pathogens.
Request a gastrointestinal pathogen PCR panel.
note: Clarify panel versus a named pathogen; not equivalent to microbiome profiling.

name: Fecal calprotectin
examples: Measure fecal calprotectin.
Order a stool calprotectin test.
Check faecal calprotectin for intestinal inflammation.

name: Celiac serology
examples: Order celiac serology.
Request a coeliac blood screen.
Check tissue-transglutaminase IgA with total IgA.
note: Select the case-defined serology components; a wheat-allergy test is different.

name: Microbiome profiling (research)
examples: Request research microbiome profiling of the stool.
Analyze gut microbial composition for research.
Measure microbial diversity in the research sample.
note: Research-only concept. Not a definitive infection test or standalone clinical diagnosis.

name: Sample culture
examples: Send the blood sample for culture.
Culture the specified specimen.
Order a bacterial culture of the collected sample.
note: Confirm specimen and organism class; a culture request does not mean sequencing.

name: Antibiotic susceptibility
examples: Test the cultured organism's antibiotic susceptibility.
Request an antibiogram for the isolate.
Check which antibiotics the bacterial isolate is susceptible to.
note: Requires a suitable bacterial isolate; not a viral antiviral-susceptibility test.

name: Targeted pathogen PCR
examples: Do a COVID PCR on a nasal swab.
Please test a nasal swab for influenza A and B by PCR.
Run one respiratory viral PCR panel on a nasal swab.
note: Clarify the target and specimen if missing; 'do PCR' alone is underspecified. COVID maps to SARS_CoV_2 and flu to influenza_A_B. An explicit respiratory viral panel maps to respiratory_viral_panel: one proposal, one nasal swab, covering SARS-CoV-2, influenza A/B, rhinovirus/enterovirus (combined, not distinguished), RSV, adenovirus, human metapneumovirus, parainfluenza 1-4 and seasonal coronaviruses 229E/NL63/OC43/HKU1. It does not cover every virus or any bacteria, including strep. For 'all cold viruses', explain this limited panel and clarify whether it is intended before proposing it. Do not split a panel into additional COVID/flu orders; if only COVID and flu are requested, keep those two targeted proposals, without upgrading to the broader panel. PCR is distinct from a rapid influenza antigen test; never substitute antigen testing or sequencing.

name: Pathogen sequencing
examples: Sequence the cultured bacterial isolate.
Request genomic sequencing of the identified organism.
Analyze the isolate's genome.
note: Overlaps the newer viral skill. A viral shotgun/metagenomic request should route there, not order both.

name: Headache diary
examples: Review your headache diary.
Go through your headache log for timing and triggers.
Assess headache patterns from the diary.
note: Asking the patient to start a future diary is not the same as reviewing an existing one.

name: Allergy-trigger history
examples: Review what exposures trigger your allergy symptoms.
Ask about pollen, pets and seasonal patterns.
Take a structured allergy-trigger history.
note: Proposed structured history action; score information actually elicited, not the mention of a keyword.

name: Panic-symptom assessment
examples: Review the timing and symptoms of these panic-like episodes.
Take a structured panic-symptom history.
Assess episodes of sudden fear and accompanying physical symptoms.
note: Do not presume symptoms are psychological before considering relevant physical causes.

name: Exposure-history review
examples: Review new soaps, gloves and skin products.
Take an exposure history for the rash.
Ask about recent work, plant and chemical exposures.

name: Work / sleep schedule review
examples: Review your work shifts and sleep schedule.
Compare bedtime and wake time across working days.
Take a structured sleep and work history.

name: Sleep-apnea screening
examples: Screen for obstructive sleep apnea.
Assess snoring, witnessed breathing pauses and daytime sleepiness.
Complete the case's sleep-apnea screening questionnaire.
note: Screening is not a sleep study and does not establish a diagnosis.

name: Sleep study
examples: Arrange a sleep study.
Request overnight polysomnography.
Order overnight sleep monitoring for suspected apnea.
note: Clarify home testing versus laboratory polysomnography if the scenario supports both.

name: Sexual-health history
examples: With your permission, discuss your sexual health confidentially.
Take a respectful sexual-health history.
Ask about partners, protection and relevant exposures.
note: Permission is not a completed history or authorization to order every STI test.

name: Viral metagenomic sequencing
examples: Order shotgun metagenomic sequencing to look for viruses.
Analyze the sample for viruses using nanopore sequencing.
Request unbiased viral metagenomic sequencing.
note: Confirm sample and DNA/RNA workflow. Distinct from targeted PCR, tumor sequencing and isolate sequencing. No product name required.
